description: France occupies the Ruhr, Germany strikes, and the mark collapses to one trillion per dollar.
content_html:
The Ruhr Crisis, 1923

By 1923, Germany had fallen behind on its reparations payments. In January 1923, French and Belgian troops marched into the Ruhr, Germany's industrial heartland, to seize coal and steel as payment in kind. The German government responded by ordering passive resistance — a general strike across the occupied zone. Workers stopped producing, officials refused to obey French orders, and sabotage became widespread. France responded with arrests, deportations and the shooting of protesters; thirteen workers died in the Krupp factory incident in Essen in March 1923.

Key Fact

The German government paid striking Ruhr workers by printing money. This decision, combined with a loss of industrial output, triggered hyperinflation: by November 1923, one US dollar was worth approximately 4.2 trillion German marks.

Hyperinflation, 1923

Hyperinflation had deep roots before 1923 — Germany had printed money to fund the First World War, and reparations demands had strained public finances since 1921 — but the passive resistance payments turned a serious inflation into a catastrophe. The government printed billions of marks to pay strikers who were producing nothing. Prices rose so fast that workers were paid twice daily and rushed to shops before prices increased again. Wheelbarrows of banknotes were required to buy bread. At the peak in November 1923, one US dollar was worth approximately 4.2 trillion marks.

The social effects were devastating but uneven. Those on fixed incomes — pensioners, civil servants, people with savings — saw their wealth wiped out. Debtors benefited: mortgage holders and factory owners who owed money could pay off their debts with near-worthless notes. Some wealthy businessmen actually gained from hyperinflation by buying up real assets cheaply. This redistribution of wealth created intense social resentment that would last for decades.

The crisis was resolved by Gustav Stresemann, who became Chancellor in August 1923. He called off passive resistance in September 1923, accepting the political cost of appearing to surrender to France, because he recognised the printing presses had to stop. In November 1923, a new currency — the Rentenmark — was introduced at a rate of one Rentenmark to one trillion old marks. The Rentenmark was backed by Germany’s land and industrial assets, giving it credibility where paper money had none. Hyperinflation ended almost immediately. The following year, Stresemann's government negotiated the Dawes Plan, which restructured reparations payments and unlocked US loans that began Germany's economic recovery.

The Munich Putsch, November 1923

The crisis of 1923 encouraged those who believed the Weimar Republic was finished. In Munich, Adolf Hitler — leader of the small Nazi Party — attempted to use the chaos to seize power. On the evening of 8 November 1923, he burst into a meeting at the Bürgerbräukeller, a large beer hall in Munich, fired a pistol into the ceiling, and declared a ‘national revolution’. He hoped to trigger a march on Berlin, modelled on Mussolini's March on Rome in 1922.

Key Fact

The Munich Putsch (8–9 November 1923) failed within 24 hours when police fired on the Nazi march at the Odeonsplatz. Sixteen Nazis and four police officers were killed. Hitler was arrested, tried, and sentenced to five years — but served only nine months, during which he dictated Mein Kampf.

The putsch failed for practical reasons: the Bavarian government and the army did not support it. Hitler had miscalculated the strength of loyalty to the republic among local authorities. However, the trial proved an unexpected propaganda gift. Hitler used the courtroom to attack the Weimar government as traitors and deliver nationalist speeches that were widely reported in the press. His light sentence — five years, of which he served nine months at Landsberg Prison — revealed the judiciary’s sympathy with right-wing nationalism.

While in prison, Hitler dictated Mein Kampf (‘My Struggle’), which outlined his ideology: extreme nationalism, anti-Semitism, the concept of Lebensraum, and the need for a dictatorial leader. He concluded that power could not be seized by force — it had to be won through the ballot box and legal means. This tactical shift would shape Nazi strategy throughout the late 1920s and early 1930s.

The year 1923 is often treated as a turning point in Weimar history precisely because multiple crises converged simultaneously. The Ruhr occupation, hyperinflation and the Munich Putsch all occurred within a single calendar year, and all three reflected the same underlying truth: Germany in 1923 was a republic in crisis, unloved by the left, hated by the right, and battered by forces largely beyond its control. That it survived — and even stabilised rapidly in 1924 with Stresemann’s currency reform and the Dawes Plan — is itself significant. The recovery that followed was real, but it rested on American loans and Stresemann’s personal diplomatic skill, both of which would disappear within six years. The psychological scars of 1923, particularly the middle class’s memory of their savings being wiped out, never fully healed and would resurface when economic crisis returned after 1929.
exam_tip_html: For a 6-mark ‘Explain a cause’ question on hyperinflation, pick one cause — such as the decision to fund passive resistance by printing money — and develop it with specific evidence (the Ruhr occupation, the scale of the money printing, the November 1923 exchange rate). Don’t just list multiple causes. For an 8-mark ‘Explain the significance’ question on the Munich Putsch, address both immediate significance (failed coup, Hitler arrested) and longer-term significance (the trial gave Hitler national publicity, Mein Kampf outlined future strategy, the light sentence showed judicial bias).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr (January 1923) triggered passive resistance; the German government printed money to fund the strike, causing hyperinflation that destroyed savings and destabilised society.
  • Hyperinflation peaked in November 1923 at approximately 4.2 trillion marks per dollar; the crisis was ended by Stresemann calling off passive resistance and introducing the Rentenmark.
  • The Munich Putsch (November 1923) failed militarily but gave Hitler national publicity; serving only nine months in prison, he used the time to write Mein Kampf and shift to a legal strategy for power.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the hyperinflation of 1923 that affected ordinary German people.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific impact (e.g. savings wiped out, prices rising so fast workers were paid twice daily, pensioners unable to afford food) with supporting detail. Secure (1–2): identifies an impact with some development. Developing (1): vague reference to people suffering. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr in 1923.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. France and Belgium sent troops in January 1923 to seize coal and steel as reparations payment in kind; German workers responded with government-backed passive resistance (general strike) that spread across the occupied zone. Secure (3): two features with some development. Developing (2): two features briefly stated. Emerging (1): one feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the hyperinflation crisis of 1923.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): identifies a clear cause (e.g. the government printed money to fund passive resistance; underlying inflation from First World War spending) AND develops it with specific evidence AND shows how it led to hyperinflation. Secure (3–4): cause identified and developed but linkage limited. Developing (2): cause stated with brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple, undeveloped point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the hyperinflation of 1923 for German society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): identifies a clear consequence (e.g. middle-class savings destroyed, fuelling resentment against Weimar; debtors benefited while creditors suffered; social instability made extremist politics more attractive) AND develops it with specific detail AND traces further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): consequence stated briefly. Emerging (1): vague mention of suffering.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Munich Putsch for the development of the Nazi Party in the years 1923 to 1929.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): significance at the time (failed putsch, 16 Nazis killed, Hitler arrested) AND over time (trial gave national publicity, light sentence, Mein Kampf written in prison, Hitler switched to legal electoral strategy). Secure (5–6): both time frames addressed with development; may be uneven. Developing (3–4): focused mainly on immediate failure or on longer term, not both. Emerging (1–2): description without analysis.

practice_questions.text: 'Hyperinflation was more damaging to the Weimar Republic than the Munich Putsch.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): sustained argument with agreement (hyperinflation: wiped out middle-class savings, caused social chaos, undermined faith in the government, made extremism more attractive) AND disagreement (Munich Putsch: gave Hitler national platform, revealed judiciary's sympathy with the right, forced tactical shift to legal strategy that ultimately succeeded in 1933). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides developed with evidence; judgement present. Developing (4–6): one side more developed; limited judgement. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

knowledge_checks.q: Why did French and Belgian troops enter the Ruhr in January 1923?
options: To prevent a German military build-up
To seize coal and steel because Germany had defaulted on reparations
To support the Weimar government against communist revolution

knowledge_checks.q: What happened to Adolf Hitler as a result of the Munich Putsch?
options: He fled Germany to avoid arrest
He was sentenced to five years but served only nine months
He was acquitted and released immediately

knowledge_checks.q: In November 1923, the German government introduced a new currency called the _____ to replace the worthless mark.
The German government's policy of _____ resistance meant workers in the Ruhr stopped producing, forcing the government to print money to pay them.
Match each event to its correct date:
left: French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr

flashcard_questions.q: When did French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr?
Why did France and Belgium occupy the Ruhr in 1923?
flashcard_questions.a: Germany had defaulted on reparations payments; they came to seize coal and steel.

flashcard_questions.q: What was 'passive resistance' in the Ruhr in 1923?
flashcard_questions.a: A government-backed general strike: workers refused to co-operate with occupying forces.

flashcard_questions.q: How did funding passive resistance cause hyperinflation?
flashcard_questions.a: The government printed money to pay striking workers, collapsing the mark's value.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the approximate exchange rate at the peak of hyperinflation in November 1923?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 4.2 trillion marks to one US dollar.

flashcard_questions.q: Who replaced the worthless mark in November 1923, and with what currency?
flashcard_questions.a: Gustav Stresemann's government introduced the Rentenmark.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Rentenmark backed by?
flashcard_questions.a: Germany's land and industrial assets, rather than gold.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Munich Putsch take place?
Where did Hitler launch the Munich Putsch?
flashcard_questions.a: At the Bürgerbraukeller beer hall in Munich.

flashcard_questions.q: What sentence did Hitler receive for the Munich Putsch?
flashcard_questions.a: Five years; he served only nine months at Landsberg Prison.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Hitler write while in prison after the Munich Putsch?
flashcard_questions.a: Mein Kampf ('My Struggle'), outlining his ideology and political goals.

flashcard_questions.q: What tactical lesson did Hitler draw from the failure of the Munich Putsch?
flashcard_questions.a: Power had to be won through elections and legal means, not by force.

glossary_terms.definition: Germany's most important industrial region, in western Germany, occupied by French and Belgian forces in January 1923 after Germany defaulted on reparations payments.
The deliberate refusal by German workers and businesses in the Ruhr to co-operate with French and Belgian occupying forces in 1923.
An extreme and rapid rise in prices that destroys the value of money; Germany experienced this in 1923 when the mark became almost worthless.
A new German currency introduced in November 1923 to replace the worthless mark, backed by the value of Germany's land and industrial assets rather than gold.
The National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP), founded in 1919 and led by Hitler from 1921, which became the dominant fascist party in Germany.
Hitler's foreign policy goal of conquering 'living space' in eastern Europe for the German people, at the expense of Slavic peoples.

items.title: Mark Felton Productions — Weimar and Nazi Germany
items.description: Mark Felton's channel covers the political and economic crises of 1920s Germany, including the hyperinflation crisis and the Munich Putsch, with primary-source detail.

items.title: Simple History — Weimar Germany and Crisis of 1923
items.description: Simple History's animated short videos explain the Ruhr crisis, passive resistance, and the collapse of the German mark in accessible form for GCSE revision.

items.title: Epic History TV — Weimar Republic
items.description: Epic History TV's narrative documentaries cover the crisis year of 1923, the Beer Hall Putsch, and Gustav Stresemann's economic stabilisation.

items.title: Downfall (2004)
items.description: German drama depicting the final collapse of the Nazi regime — understanding Hitler's rise requires understanding the 1923 crises that first propelled him to national attention.

items.title: Metropolis (1927)
items.description: Fritz Lang's 1927 Weimar masterpiece, made during the fragile recovery after hyperinflation — a primary cultural artefact of the period students are studying.

items.title: German Inflation 1923 — Spartacus Educational
items.description: Primary source accounts and detailed analysis of how hyperinflation destroyed middle-class savings and destabilised Weimar politics.

items.title: Ruhr Occupation 1923 — Spartacus Educational
items.description: Documents the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr, German passive resistance, and how the crisis triggered both hyperinflation and the Beer Hall Putsch.

items.title: Beer Hall Putsch — Spartacus Educational
items.description: Primary sources on Hitler's November 1923 coup attempt, his trial, and his decision to pursue electoral rather than violent routes to power.

items.title: Hyperinflation — Britannica
items.description: Britannica's analysis of hyperinflation, including the German case of 1921–23 where monthly inflation peaked at roughly 29,500%.

items.title: Beer Hall Putsch — Britannica
items.description: Britannica's account of Hitler's abortive November 1923 coup, its suppression, and the trial that gave him a national platform.
